data: Philosophical, Aesthetic, and Social Dimensions in Bhakti: An Introduction

This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the tradition of Bhakti as an embodied practice of attention, to understand one’s relation with self, the divine, and the world. Through close readings of poetry, song, and performance across diverse Bhakti traditions (translated and in original wherever available), students will learn how to listen to various shades of expression of bhakti and what it implies; ultimately reaching an understanding that devotion, indeed, is an inadequate translation of it.
The course explores regional and vernacular Bhakti traditions through the voices of female saints like Meera, Andal, Akka Mahadevi, and Janabai. Listening to their poetry and songs in class will help students reflect on love, desire, and the subversion of social and gender norms. We then turn to Nirgun (Formless) Bhakti and the radical critiques of Kabir and Ravidas, examining their challenges to caste, ritualism, and hypocrisy, and their vision of an anti-caste world. Listening becomes a critical mode of engaging with Bhakti across its diverse textual and performance contexts. The course concludes with the introspective poetry of Lalla Ded (Lalla) of Kashmir and the living musical tradition of the Bauls of Bengal.
Drawing from religious studies, literary studies, ethnomusicology, gender studies, the course uses poetry, song, performance recordings, live performances, and films to facilitate a participatory understanding of Bhakti. Students will listen, participate in singing, read, and reflect not only on texts and performance, but also on the sensory and affective worlds they create.
Visiting Assistant Professor, Centre for Writing and Pedagogy
